newsitem.title: FRANCE: PSA Peugeot Citroen first half profit slashed.
newsitem.headline: PSA Peugeot Citroen first half profit slashed.

text.p: French carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen on Monday reported its profit more than halved in the first six months of 1996 as a brutal price war in France took a heavy toll on the domestic car industry.

The company reported its net attributable profit fell to 602 million French francs ($117.2 million) in the first half from 1.22 billion in the same period last year. Its operating margin shrank to 1.34 billion francs from 2.78 billion.
Its stock fell 2.4 percent to close at 569 francs. Analysts found the results disappointing but not surprising.
Peugeot's French rival, Renault SA, earlier this month reported a huge drop in first-half profit to 158 million francs from 1.76 billion and predicted a loss for the year.
French carmakers are struggling in a tough environment as their home market has turned into the biggest battleground of a fierce price war among European and U.S. manufacturers.
Foreign carmakers are attracted by the rapid growth of French car sales, buoyed by the state's new-cars-for-old incentive scheme, and the high costs of French companies.
Car sales in France rose 7.4 percent in the first eight months of the year, but foreigners took the lion's share of the increase, registering a combined 20 percent sales gain.

"Foreigners have become very aggressive. For them France is a foreign market and they can even afford to lose money here because for them it's a strategic issue," said a car analyst at a French brokerage house.
Foreign companies, notably Italy's Fiat, have benefited from the French incentive scheme, which has tended to favour sales of smaller cars with smaller profit margins.
PSA Peugeot Citroen said in a statement its first-half performance was also hurt by the franc's strength relative to other currencies such as the Italian lira and British pound.
"In this context, PSA Peugeot Citroen sought the best balance between unit margins and volumes," in a bid to maintain market share while limiting the erosion of its profit margins, the company said.

The Peugeot group has withstood the ravages better than its domestic rival Renault, which now looks to be the weakest of Europe's big six carmakers. Analysts say the Peugeot group has tighter control over its costs and a clearer strategy.

Although its unit sales rose just one percent, turnover increased three percent to 89.04 billion francs as it enhanced its product mix and sold more expensive models in its line-up, including the new Peugeot 406 sedan launched last autumn.
Its balance sheet looks good. Cashflow of 6.66 billion francs more than covered 5.29 billion francs of investment.
"It's a good company in a terrible environment, and right now, the environment is more important," one analyst said.

The company said recent currency shifts -- slight gains in the lira and lower French interest rates -- will help its second-half results, prompting at least one French brokerage house to raise its 1996 earnings estimate for the group.
But the French car industry faces an uncertain outlook.
Car sales in France are surging ahead of the expiry on September 30 of the rebate scheme, but they are then expected to fall if new underpinnings are not put in place. ($1=5.135 French Franc)
